Title: Diagnosis
Details: The test failure relates to the XPath expression involving the axis preceding::node(), which should select any kind of node, not only elements or documents. The current bug report indicates a known issue in DOMNodePointer.java where the node() test implementation only returns true for element nodes or the document node. However, per XPath semantics, node() should match any type of node.

The report suggests the following code snippet in DOMNodePointer:

```java
case Compiler.NODE_TYPE_NODE :
   return nodeType == Node.ELEMENT_NODE || nodeType == Node.DOCUMENT_NODE;
```

This is too restrictive and excludes other node types like text nodes, comments, processing instructions, etc., which node() should include. The report proposes this be changed to always return true for NODE_TYPE_NODE, i.e.

```java
case Compiler.NODE_TYPE_NODE :
   return true;
```

This aligns with the XPath specification that node() matches any node.

The failing test case `testAxisPreceding()` exercises an XPath with `preceding::node()[3]`, which would fail if only elements and documents are considered matching nodes but exclude text nodes (like text() nodes under employeeCount). Since the reported method is part of the DOM model, a similar issue likely exists in the JDOM model as well, which the report hints at ("Same in JDOMNodePo").

The recent relevant bugs do not address this same node-matching logic, so the diagnosis focuses on this fundamental bug in the node type test handling.

In summary, the bug is that the node test for XPath node() in the DOM and JDOM node pointer implementations improperly restricts nodes matched to elements and document nodes only, instead of all nodes, causing incorrect XPath evaluation for expressions involving node() like the failing preceding::node()[3] test.

Fixing this logic to return true for all node types when node() is requested should resolve this test failure and align behavior with XPath semantics.

Next, I will suggest methods likely to contain this faulty node type check.
